cim: Best AI Stocks to Buy in 2026: 10 Top Picks & How to Invest
cim_eredeti: Best AI Stocks to Buy in 2026: 10 Top Picks & How to Invest
szoveg_eredeti:
AI stocks are at the forefront of the AI revolution as artificial intelligence is reshaping industries and driving real revenue growth for the companies building and powering it. From chips and cloud infrastructure to software and automation, AI is becoming a core competitive advantage.

Below are some of the top AI stocks to consider buying now, followed by tips on how to invest in the space.

Almost every tech stock is an AI stock these days as the technology spans from semiconductors to cloud computing to software and other industries. That includes stocks like Nvidia, Alphabet, Microsoft, CoreWeave, Meta Platforms, Adobe, Alibaba, Amazon, Palantir, and Oracle, all of which are among the top AI stocks to buy now.

Nvidia (NVDA -4.27%) has become the backbone of the AI revolution. Its graphics processing units (GPUs) are the industry standard for training and running large language models, making the company one of the earliest and biggest beneficiaries of generative AI.

Once known primarily for gaming chips, Nvidia now supplies the core hardware for AI data centers worldwide. Its data center segment generates the vast majority of its revenue, fueled by surging demand from cloud computing providers and AI start-ups. Elon Musk just declared its new Vera Rubin architecture to be the best, saying SpaceX would build exclusively on Nvidia.

Revenue has exploded since 2022, with full-year sales reaching $215.9 billion in 2025, up 65% year over year, and revenue growth has accelerated in 2026 as well. Nvidia has expanded beyond chips, offering full-stack AI infrastructure that includes networking, software, and systems designed to run AI workloads at scale.

After the blowout success of its Blackwell platform, Nvidia is now rolling out the next-generation Rubin platform in the second half of 2026, which includes the updated Vera CPU. Demand continues to outstrip supply, underscoring Nvidia’s dominant position.

Beyond data centers, Nvidia is investing in autonomous vehicles, robotics, and “physical AI.” These initiatives remain a small part of revenue today, but they could become meaningful growth drivers for Nvidia over time.

Following revelations that CEO Jensen Huang had a relationship with a suspected Chinese spy, the stock is facing a unique threat. Investors shouldn't ignore it as it could hang over the company for months and the consequences could be significant.

Alphabet (GOOGL +1.18%) (GOOG +0.73%) has been investing in artificial intelligence for more than a decade, highlighted by its acquisition of DeepMind in 2014. Today, AI touches nearly every part of its business.

The company’s Gemini models power products across Google Search, YouTube, Google Cloud, and Workspace. Though investors have worried that generative AI could threaten Google Search, advertising revenue continues to grow steadily. Additionally, its Google Cloud business is soaring thanks in part to AI-driven demand.

Alphabet is also a leader in autonomous driving through Waymo, which operates fully driverless ride-hailing services in multiple U.S. cities. On the infrastructure side, Alphabet designs its own AI chips, known as TPUs, putting it in direct competition with Nvidia in certain workloads.

In 2026, Alphabet is now planning $195-$205 billion in capital spending, much of it aimed at AI infrastructure. With information and data at its core, Alphabet remains one of the most deeply integrated AI companies in the world.

Microsoft's (MSFT +2.75%) partnership with OpenAI has made it one of the most visible players in AI. The company began investing in OpenAI in 2019 and now owns a significant minority stake following the start-up’s restructuring.

AI is embedded across Microsoft’s ecosystem, from Azure cloud services to Microsoft 365 Copilot, Edge, and GitHub. Azure AI Foundry has seen rapid adoption, with approximately 80% of Fortune 500 companies using the service.

Microsoft has also diversified its AI strategy by supporting multiple internal and third-party models across its platforms, reducing reliance on any single partner. Azure AI Foundry, launched in late 2024, allows customers to build and manage AI applications and agents, and adoption has grown quickly.

Microsoft also owns a significant stake in OpenAI, which was valued at 27% before a recent funding round. With OpenAI planning to go public in early 2027, Microsoft could be in line for a big payday.

CoreWeave (CRWV +5.56%) may be the closest thing to a pure-play AI infrastructure stock. The company’s cloud platform was designed specifically for AI workloads and counts customers like Nvidia, OpenAI, Microsoft, and Meta among its core clients.

Revenue growth has been explosive. CoreWeave went from minimal sales in 2022 to $5.1 billion in 2025 and is expected to generate more than $10 billion in revenue in 2026.

That growth comes with risk. Microsoft accounted for 67% of revenue in 2025. The company carries heavy debt and large capital expenditures, and it's deeply unprofitable. Nearly all of CoreWeave’s revenue is directly tied to AI demand. News in July that Meta Platforms would launch its own cloud computing business sent the stock tumbling, showing it may be at a competitive disadvantage next to the Facebook parent. It's also been under pressure as investors have been skeptical of the hyperscaler spending ramp, including its rising bond yields.

For investors seeking direct exposure to AI infrastructure, CoreWeave offers high upside but elevated risk.

Meta Platforms (META +5.12%) doesn’t operate a cloud platform, though the company said it would begin to offer some cloud services. Still, it's more focused on using AI compute for its own needs, including its Superintelligence Labs.

In September, the company appeared to have its first breakthrough on that front with the Meta Muse personal AI agent, an app that can handle things like travel booking, financial organization, and even negotiating for a discount. The app has ranked #1 for weeks and topped 5 million downloads in less than a month. It also drove a surge in the stock.

Meta has also invested heavily in AI across advertising, consumer apps, and hardware, and it's targeting $135 billion-$145 billion in capex spending in 2026, with much of that going into AI. Meta AI is embedded across Facebook, Instagram, and WhatsApp and reached 1 billion monthly active users in 2025.

AI plays a growing role in ad targeting and creative tools, and Meta aims to automate much of the advertising process using AI. The company has also introduced a new AI model, Muse Spark, which has received positive reviews and is an improvement over the previous Llama models.

Beyond software, Meta is incorporating AI into devices like Ray-Ban smart glasses and Meta Quest headsets. The company sees AI as central to its long-term strategy across experiences, advertising, and hardware.

Adobe (ADBE -0.83%) has successfully integrated AI into its creative software ecosystem. Adobe Firefly, its suite of generative AI tools are designed to enhance, not replace, creative work, and Adobe has taken a cautious approach to training models using licensed and public data.

More than 24 billion images and related creations have been generated using Firefly since its 2023 launch. Adobe has also expanded into agentic AI, offering tools that improve productivity for marketing, analytics, and operations teams.

While Adobe’s growth has slowed in recent years, it remains a dominant player in creative and marketing software and is well-positioned to benefit from AI adoption across enterprise teams.

Alibaba (BABA -3.72%) has broad exposure to AI through cloud computing, e-commerce, and logistics. Its Qwen family of large language models underpins a rebuilt AI-focused cloud platform, and the company plans to invest more than $50 billion in AI infrastructure.
